title: Umar, al-Faruq
hookLine: fierce, just, the one who distinguishes right and wrong

cards: Near the Ka'ba is a spot the Qur'an calls the place where Abraham stood. Umar once said to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: why don't we take the place where Abraham stood as a place of prayer?
And then, Umar says in Bukhari, a verse came down. In Pickthall's words: "Take as your place of worship the place where Abraham stood (to pray)." Pilgrims still pray there.
Umar had his own way of putting it: my Lord agreed with me. Today: the man they called al-Faruq.

teach.b: In that report, Umar names three things where, he said, his Lord agreed with him: the place of prayer by Abraham's stone, the screening of the Prophet's wives, and a warning to them in a quarrel at home.
He isn't boasting. He is remembering moments when what he thought was fair and what was revealed turned out to match.
Al-Faruq means the one who distinguishes, who separates true from false, right from wrong. Sources differ on who first called him that. The Prophet said striking things about him.
In one report in Bukhari, he tells Umar that whenever Satan meets him on a road, Satan takes a different road.
In another, he says that earlier nations had people who were inspired, and if there were one in his community, it would be Umar.
This is the same Umar who, in Ibn Ishaq's telling, had once set out to harm the Prophet, and then came into Islam himself. The fierceness didn't go away. It got pointed in a new direction.
Later, as caliph, he was remembered as a judge.

teach.h: SEAT THE STRONG AND WEAK ALIKE.
teach.b: A letter on judging is attributed to him, telling a governor to treat people equally: in how you look at them, where you seat them, and how you rule, so the powerful don't hope you'll lean their way and the weak don't lose hope in your fairness.
Sunni Muslims honor Umar as the second caliph. Shia Muslims view his part in the succession differently, and remember him in another light.
What the name al-Faruq asks of anyone is plain: see the difference, then act on it.

how: Sunni Muslims honor Umar ibn al-Khattab as the second caliph and tell stories of his justice, while Shia Muslims view his role in the succession differently.

o: the one who tells right from wrong
the one who was first to believe
the one who rides out ahead in battle

p: taken as a place of prayer
seat the strong and weak alike

s: Umar asked for Abraham's place to be a place of prayer, and a verse came
al-Baqarah 125: take as your place of worship the place where Abraham stood.
everyone agrees the Prophet gave him the name al-Faruq
sources differ on who first called him that.
Umar was gentle from the start
he had set out to harm the Prophet before he came into Islam; the fierceness was turned in a new direction.

games.q: you're a judge in Umar's letter. a powerful man and a poor man stand before you. where do you seat them?
o: the powerful man nearer, out of respect.
the poor man nearer, out of pity.
both alike, in look, seat and ruling.
games.why: the letter says treat them equally, so the strong don't hope you'll lean their way and the weak don't lose hope.

practice: Bring to mind a small decision where people's interests pull against each other: who gets the last seat, who does the chore, whose side you take in a family argument.

Try Umar's letter: seat everyone at the same height in your mind, and ask what you'd decide if you liked them all equally. If you pray, ask Allah to show you the difference between what's comfortable and what's fair.

wordCard.voice: Al-Faruq. The one who distinguishes, who tells right from wrong and true from false: the title Umar is known by. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the one who distinguishes, who separates right from wrong.

carryVoice: Your line: the one who distinguished. All that fierceness, pointed toward fairness. See you tomorrow.
